Ka'anna is the light form of the heavy one, and its noun is the pronoun of the woman or the pronoun of the matter. Zabiyatun is nominative according to the first, as a predicate; according to the second, it is the subject, and with its predicate it is the predicate of kana. Ta'tu is an attribute according to the first and the predicate according to the second. It is also narrated as zabiyatan (accusative), making it the noun even though its operation is slightly weakened. It is also narrated in the genitive after the kaf, with inna as an extra particle between the preposition and its object:

Ta'tu: takes and grasps, inclining toward the leaves of the acacia. Among the rare forms: awraqa, so he is wariq; and a'naʿa, so he is yani'. The analogical form would be muwriq, meaning abundant in leaves. It is also narrated as nadir instead of wariq. Al-salm: acacia trees. This is her condition on one day; and on another day she annoys us, wanting our wealth added to hers, so if we give her, she does not let us sleep from the abundance of her talk and her harassment, and she does not sleep either.

Here, al-yawm means unrestricted time.]]

The clause has the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal): i.e., he becomes like one who does not hear. "Wa-idha balaghahu shay'un min ayatina wa-alima annahu minha ittakhadhaha" — i.e., he takes the signs as a mockery (huzuwan). He did not say "ittakhadhahu" (taking it), to indicate that when he senses something of the speech to be among the signs which Allah the Exalted sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ), he plunges into mocking all the signs, and does not limit his mockery to what has reached him. It may also mean: if he knows of Our signs something that the obstinate can cling to, and find a pretext to climb upon it for attack and slander, he seizes upon it and takes the signs of Allah as a mockery. This is like the seizing of Ibn al-Za'bara upon the saying of the Exalted, "Innakum wa-ma ta'buduna min duni Allahi hasabu jahannam," and his deceiving the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his saying, "I have defeated you." It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to a thing (shay'), because it has the sense of the verse, as in the saying of Abu al-Atahiya:

Nafsi bi-shay'in min al-dunya mu'allaqatun... Allahu wa-l-qa'imu al-mahdiyyu yakfiha [[Nafsi bi-shay'in min al-dunya mu'allaqatun, Allahu wal-qa'imu al-mahdiyyu yakfiha.
Inni la-ay'asu minha thumma yut'iminy... fiha ihtiqaruka lil-dunya wa-ma fiha.

By Abu al-Atahiya. By "thing" he means a slave-girl among the concubines of al-Mahdi, named Utba, and for this reason he returned the pronoun to it in the feminine. His saying "min al-dunya" means that he does not desire from the world other than her. "Al-qa'im" means: the one who upholds the Law. "Yakfiha" means: it suffices me for that need, or it suffices my soul what it desires. "Allahu" is with a cut hamza, because the beginning of the hemistich is a place of starting a sentence. "Inni la-ay'asu" means: I cut off my hope from her, then I hope for her again because of your contempt for the world and what is in it. This is praise of the utmost generosity. It is related that he wrote that in a garment, placed it in a jar, and presented it to al-Mahdi. He was about to hand it to him, but she said: "Will you hand me to a man who earns his living by love?" So he ordered the jar filled with money and gave it to him. He said to the treasurers: "Only dinars were commanded for me." They said: "We will give you dirhams and return to him." They disputed about that for a year. She said: "If he were a lover, he would not have separated them."]]

Referring to Utba. It is read: "ulaika" (those), a reference to every affak athim, since it includes the liars. Al-wara' is a name for the direction that a person conceals from behind or in front. The poet said:

Alaysa wara'i an taraakhat manIyyati... adibbu ma'a al-wildan azhafu ka'l-nasr [[By Ubayd; the hamza is for confirmation. Wara'i here means "in front of me," though originally it is the direction that a person conceals, but it is common for the direction behind him, and it was extended until it was used for every unseen thing, and from it: the future. Tarakhat: became distant and delayed. Adibbu: I walk gently and slowly. The anna is implied before it, since it is the noun of laysa, even though its form is nominative. Azhafu may be an apposition, or a circumstantial clause. Ka'l-nasr is a circumstantial clause, or its meaning is: like the crawl of the eagle on the ground, along with its whiteness. There is in it a kind of precaution, because "ma'a al-wildan" might suggest a deficiency of intellect, so it indicates that the intended meaning is weakness like children. White hair is like the eagle, because it is white, while the eagle is the chief of birds and all birds fear it.]]

From it is His saying, the Exalted: "min warā'ihim," i.e., from before them, "ma kasabu" — what they gathered of wealth in their journeys and their trade — "wa-la ma ittakhadhu min duni Allahi" — nor what they took besides Allah, i.e., the idols.

This is a reference to the Qur'an, indicated by His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of their Lord﴾, because the signs of their Lord are the Qur'an. That is, this Qur'an is complete in guidance, just as you say: Zayd is a man (rajul), meaning he is complete in manliness.

وأيما رجل. Al-rijz (severe punishment) is the most intense torment. It has been read with the genitive (jarr) of أليم and with its nominative (raf').

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 45, verse 12–13:

﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ through trade, or through diving for pearls and coral, and extracting fresh flesh (fish), and other benefits of the sea.

If you ask: what is the meaning of "minhu" (مِنْهُ) in His saying ﴿all of it from Him﴾ (جَمِيعاً مِنْهُ), and what is its position in terms of i'rab (grammatical construction)? I answer: it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning is: He subjected these things, as being from Him and originating from His side, that is, He is the one who brought them into being and originated them by His power and wisdom, and then made them subservient to His creation.

It is also permissible that it be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), its estimate being: ﴿they are all from Him﴾. And it is permissible that ﴿and He has subjected for you﴾ (وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمْ) be an emphasis of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He has subjected for you﴾ (سَخَّرَ لَكُمْ), then the statement begins: ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, all of it from Him﴾ (ما فِي السَّماواتِ وَما فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً مِنْهُ). And it is permissible that "ما فِي الْأَرْضِ" (whatever is in the earth) be the subject (mubtada'), and "مِنْهُ" its predicate (khabar).

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "minnatan" (مِنَّةً, as a favour), and Salama ibn Muḥārib read "minhu" (مِنْهُ), on the basis that "minhu" is the agent (fā'il) of "sakhkhara" (subjected) according to figurative attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī). Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: that (ḏālika) is from Him.

Or it is from Him.

The omitted speech is left out because the answer indicates it. The meaning is: say to them, "Forgive, so that they may forgive," [they do not hope for the Days of Allah]. Lā yarjūna ayyāma Allāh means they do not expect the events (waqā'i') of Allah against His enemies, from the way the Arabs used "ayyām al-'Arab" for their battles. It is also said: they do not look forward to the times that Allah appointed for the reward of the believers and for their promised triumph therein. It is said that it was revealed before the verse of fighting, and then its ruling was abrogated (naskh). It is also said that it was revealed concerning ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, when a man from Ghifar reviled him and he intended to seize him.

It is narrated on the authority of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab: "We were in the presence of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, when a reciter recited this verse, and ʿUmar said: 'Let ʿUmar be recompensed for what he did.'"

Liyajziya (so that He may recompense) gives the reason for the command to forgive: that is, they were only commanded to forgive so that Allah may fulfil for them, as a recompense for their forgiveness, what He willed on the Day of Resurrection.

If you ask: why is qawman (a people) indefinite, when He meant those who believed, who are definite? I answer: it is praise for them and commendation of them, as if it were said: "so that He may recompense whatever people (ayyamā qawm) and a people (wa-qawman) who are specially chosen," for their patience and their overlooking the harm of their enemies among the disbelievers, and for what the disbelievers made them swallow of distress. It is also recited as "hadhihi basa'ir" (these are insights), meaning: these verses.

Am (here introducing a disjunctive question, munqati'a)? The meaning of the hamza in it is a denial of supposing. Al-ijtirah means earning, and from it comes al-jawarih (the limbs, i.e., the instruments of earning), and "fulan jarihat ahlihi" means: he is the earner for his family.

An-naj'alahum: an-nusayyirahum (that We make them). It is from ja'ala, which is transitive to two objects: the first is the pronoun (-hum), and the second is the kaf (-ka, i.e., the kaf of the verb's object). The clause "sawa'an mahyahum wa mamatuhum" (equal are their life and their death) is a substitute (badal) for the kaf, because the clause would occur as a second object, so it has the status of a singular noun. Do you not see that if you said, "an najʿalahum sawa'an mahyahum wa mamatuhum," it would be correct, just as you say, "zanantu Zaydan abuhu muntaliq" (I thought Zayd, his father is departing)?

As for the one who reads sawa'an in the accusative (naṣb), he treats sawa' as "mustawiyan" (equal, level), and mahyahum wa mamatuhum is raised as the subject (fa'il), and it is a singular noun, not a clause. As for the one who reads wa mamatuhum in the accusative, he makes mahyahum and mamatuhum two adverbs of time/place (zarfayn), like "muqaddam al-hajj" (the arrival of the pilgrims) and "khafuq an-najm" (the setting of the star). That is: equal in their life and in their death.

The meaning is a denial that the evildoers and the good-doers be equal in life, and that they be equal in death, because their conditions differ in life: these lived in the performance of acts of obedience, and those in committing sins; and in death: these died with the glad tidings of mercy and the attainment of God's reward and His pleasure, and those in despair of God's mercy and in facing the terror of what has been prepared for them.

It was said: its meaning is a denial that they be equal in death as they were equal in life, because the evildoers and the good-doers are equal in their life regarding provision and health, and they only differ in death. It was also said: "sawa'an mahyahum wa mamatuhum" is a resumed (mustaʾnaf) statement, meaning: the life of the evildoers and their death are equal, and likewise the life of the good-doers and their death: each dies according to how he lived.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 45, verses 27–31:

The governing element of the accusative in "On the Day the Hour is established" (yawma taqumu, يَوْمَ تَقُومُ) is "will lose" (yakhsar, يخسر). "On that day" (yawma'idhin, يَوْمَئِذٍ) is a substitute (badal) for "On the Day the Hour is established" (yawma taqumu). "Kneeling" (jathiyah, جاثِيَةً) means crouching, poised upon the knees. It has also been read as "jadhiyah" (جاذية). Al-judhu' (الجذوّ) is a stronger form of crouching than al-juthu' (الجثوّ), because the one who is jadhi (الجاذى) sits on the tips of his toes. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, [it is reported that] "jathiyah" means "gathered together." From Qatadah: "groups (jama'at) from al-juthwah (الجثوة), which is the group (al-jama'ah), and its plural is juthan (جثى)."

In a hadith [this is a fragment of a hadith of al-Harith ibn al-Harith al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever calls to the calls of the Jahiliyyah, he is among the juthan of Hell... the hadith." It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ahmad, and Abu Ya'la. Note: the author (al-Musannif) cited it as evidence that juthan is the plural of juthwah, which means a group.
